tier_reason: linux_single.qbk compares spreadsort vs std::sort, gives GCC 6.3 and the i7-5820K hardware, and ties the integer table to in-repo benchmark/single/benchmark_numbers.cpp. The run script benchmark/single/runGCC_benchmark_numbers.sh builds it with g++ -std=c++11 -march=native -O3; benchmark_strings.cpp and benchmark_objects.cpp are also in the repo.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 6.3 on Linux; in-repo run scripts (benchmark/single/runGCC_benchmark_*.sh) compile with g++ -std=c++11 -march=native -w -fno-operator-names -O3 -s
corrections.claimed_speedup: spreadsort ~1.94x faster than std::sort on 100M random 64-bit ints (8.2154s vs 4.2248s); the in-repo benchmark_numbers.cpp table on the same page gives 8.21s vs 4.26s (~1.93x). ~2.57x faster on 10M random strings (6.2442s vs 2.4323s); ~1.62x faster on 100M 8-byte objects with a heavy comparator (8.25s vs 5.10s). spreadsort is slower than std::sort on fully reverse-sorted ints (1.87s vs 1.36s).
corrections.caveats: Benchmark authored by the library's own maintainers, not an independent third party. The 4-decimal integer, string and object figures come from 'complex' benchmarks that the doc says are not included in the library (non-free software); the reproducible in-repo benchmark_numbers.cpp gives near-identical integer results. Flags come from the in-repo run scripts, not the doc text. Hardware (i7-5820K) and GCC 6.3 date to ~2017 and have not been re-run on recent toolchains. spreadsort is slower than std::sort on reverse-sorted input, and pdqsort (also in Boost.Sort) is about as fast as spreadsort on random ints.

notes: Numbers verified exactly in doc/linux_single.qbk. Default branch (develop) last commit is 2026-04-11; the record's 2026-08-12 matches repo pushed_at, not a commit on the default branch. License API field is null, but README and file headers state Boost Software License 1.0 (BSL-1.0), so the license is correct.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed ESA 2017 paper states GCC 6.2.0, -march=native -O3 and the three machines, and compares against GCC introsort (std-sort). The ips4o/ips4o repo has no benchmark code (only src/example.cpp), and the paper links SaschaWitt/ips4o. The separate ips4o/ips4o-benchmark-suite is not linked from the repo README and targets the later 4-machine version, so tier A is not met.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Sequential: per the Figure 6 discussion (Uniform 64-bit doubles), std-sort (GCC introsort) and DualPivot are at least 1.86x slower than IS4o for n=2^32; vs the closest competitor BlockQuicksort, IS4o is 1.14x faster on Intel2S, 1.22x on Intel4S and 1.57x on AMD1S. Parallel (n>=2^26, Uniform): IPS4o beats its closest non-in-place competitors on average by 2.26x on Intel2S (1.69x AMD1S) and its closest in-place competitors (TBB, GCC parallel-mode MCSTL quicksorts) on average by 2.78x (1.98x AMD1S); only 1.41x on Intel4S. Abstract: up to 3x vs the closest in-place competitor, and up to 1.5x vs BlockQuicksort sequentially.
corrections.hardware: One AMD Ryzen 1800 8-core, 32 GiB (AMD1S; not a Threadripper); 2x Intel Xeon E5-2683 v4 16-core, 512 GiB (Intel2S); 4x Intel Xeon E5-4640 8-core, 512 GiB (Intel4S)
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the peer-reviewed ESA 2017 paper (Section 5, Figures 6-8), which used the older SaschaWitt/ips4o code. The ips4o/ips4o repo contains no benchmark code. A separate ips4o/ips4o-benchmark-suite (GPL-3.0) has a std::sort target but is not linked from the repo README and matches the later 4-machine journal version. ips4o/ips4o is a GitHub fork of the now-deprecated SaschaWitt/ips4o and is the maintained successor. The 1.86x std::sort factor applies at n=2^32; DualPivot beats IS4o on AlmostSorted input by 1.70x, and IS4o is slower than BlockQuicksort for n<=2^15. The parallel advantage shrinks to ~1.41x on the 4-socket Intel4S machine.

notes: The record misattributed the 1.86x std::sort factor to Intel4S. The 1.57x figure is IS4o vs BlockQuicksort on AMD1S, not vs std::sort, and the 2.78x is an average, not 'up to'. GitHub reports ips4o/ips4o as fork=true with parent SaschaWitt/ips4o (167 stars, README says it is deprecated in favor of ips4o/ips4o). Metadata checks out otherwise: BSD-2-Clause, 135 stars, last commit 2025-01-15 (stale).

tier_reason: perf_charts.png plots LearnedSort vs Std::sort on 50M keys. The in-repo benchmark src/main_synth.cc (Google Benchmark, StdSort target) is built by CMakeLists.txt in Release with -O3 -march=native -mavx. The README states GCC 9.3.0 and the Xeon Gold 6150 machine; the work was also peer-reviewed at SIGMOD 2020.

corrections.caveats: The README gives no benchmark numbers in text. The speedups were read off the bar chart (plots/perf_charts.png), so they are visual estimates, not exact printed figures. On Sorted, ReverseSorted and Identical inputs, IS4o is as fast as or faster than LearnedSort. The README says LearnedSort handles only numeric keys: no payloads (records) and no string keys. No commits since 2021; this is an unmaintained academic research prototype.

notes: The chart confirms the estimates: Uniform ~1130ms vs ~5000ms (~4.4x), other random distributions ~4.2-4.6x, and Sorted/Reverse/Identical ~50ms vs ~750-1000ms. The repo was transferred from learnedsystems/LearnedSort (that URL redirects here). Metadata verified: GPL-3.0, 81 stars, not a fork, last commit 2021-08-20 (abandoned).

tier_reason: The README gives object_qsort vs std::sort numbers, and in-repo benchmark code (benchmarks/bench-objsort.hpp) exists. The README states only 'a processor with AVX-512', with no CPU model, compiler or flags, so tier A fails. The numbers are first-party and not peer-reviewed, so tier B also fails.

corrections.caveats: The README does not state the CPU model, compiler or flags for the object_qsort chart, only 'a processor with AVX-512'. Benchmark code is in benchmarks/bench-objsort.hpp (run with --benchmark_filter=*obj*). Numbers are first-party and not from an independent third party. object_qsort needs O(N) extra space for keys and indexes. An independent 2023 analysis (Voultapher sort-research-rs, intel_avx512 writeup) reported worse-than-O(N log N) scaling of the AVX-512 qsort on a random_p5 pattern; this may be fixed in later releases.

notes: claimed_speedup matches the README text exactly (up to 5x for 32-bit, ~4x for 64-bit, up to 10x for Euclidean distance). Metadata verified: BSD-3-Clause, 1,027 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-06-25 (active). A third-party benchmark of the primitive qsort vs std::sort exists at sort-research-rs, but its std::sort numbers were not extracted here.

tier_reason: The README benchmarks table compares fluxsort vs std::stable_sort using the in-repo src/bench.c, compiled with g++ -O3 -w -fpermissive on GCC 7.5.0. Hardware is not stated, so tier A fails. The benchmark is first-party, with no peer-reviewed or independent third-party suite, so tier B fails.

corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark suite (same author and suite as quadsort/wolfsort; code in src/bench.c). Hardware/CPU is not stated, and the toolchain is an old GCC 7.5.0 on WSL/Ubuntu 18.04. No peer-reviewed or independent benchmark against std::stable_sort was found; the Voultapher sort-research-rs writeups checked compare fluxsort only against Rust sorts.

notes: Numbers verified exactly: random 32-bit 0.006113s vs 0.001906s (~3.2x), ascending 0.000804s vs 0.000044s (~18x). Random 64-bit is 0.006008s vs 0.002032s (~3.0x). Record tier B was not supported, because the source is the author's own README. Metadata verified: Unlicense, 749 stars, not a fork, last commit 2024-07-27 (stale).
